articles.title: In 2018, Silvia Grecco narrated Palmeiras matches to her blind son; after their story went viral, FIFA named her its 2019 Best Fan
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring journey of Silvia Grecco, who narrates Palmeiras football matches for her blind son, Nickollas, and how their story captured hearts worldwide, leading to Silvia receiving FIFA's 2019 Best Fan award.
articles.body: A football stadium is loud, fast, and mostly visual. Play shifts across the pitch in seconds and fans follow it with their eyes while the crowd’s reaction builds around them. For a blind fan, the stadium experience can be little more than a cacophony of shouting and cheering that bears no obvious relation to the action on the pitch. Radio commentary would usually help, but it assumes the listener can already picture the game. A Brazilian mother found a way to fill that gap. What began as a private habit between her and her son eventually travelled the world and won her an award from FIFA.Silvia Grecco’s narration at PalmeirasSilvia Grecco took her son Nickollas to Palmeiras matches in São Paulo and described the game as it unfolded, from individual players’ movements to the mood in the stands. According to FIFA, the tradition started when Nickollas, after a few visits to the stadium, took off his radio headset and listened to the fans chanting without knowing what was happening around him. Silvia began describing the action to him and said she tried to convey the emotion of a mother as well as a fan.Nickollas’s birth and adoptionAccording to FIFA, Nickollas was born five months early, weighing about half a kilogram. Complications during birth meant his retina did not develop, leaving him blind. He was also diagnosed with mild autism. Aleteia reported that twelve other couples waiting to adopt had passed him over before Silvia adopted him and it gave his age as eleven when it published its report in September 2019.The 2021 systematic review on sport and inclusionA systematic review titled Influence of Physical Activity and Sport on the Inclusion of People with Visual Impairment, published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health on 31 December 2021, examined what shared sport can do socially. In their conclusion, the authors found that sport programmes help improve attitudes towards people with disabilities and increase social skills. The review also found that visually impaired people tend to feel excluded at some point while taking part in sport and that blind people tend to be less physically active than their sighted counterparts, with accessibility often a key issue.The FIFA Fan Award, 23 September 2019FIFA featured Silvia and Nickollas as the first story in its six-part Sheroes series and nominated her for the Fan Award. Football fans from around the world voted for Silvia and her story won the award with 58.36 per cent of the vote, according to Reuters. The award was handed out at The Best FIFA Football Awards held at Teatro alla Scala, Milan, on 23 September 2019.Nickollas accompanied her to the event. Silvia said she had felt invisible for many years, but that things had changed since the Sheroes video was published, because people now know that disabled people exist and that sport can change their lives. CNN Chile reported that Palmeiras invited them to a training session, where coach Luiz Felipe Scolari introduced Nickollas to the players. Her narration let one blind fan follow the match from the stands and the attention it drew has highlighted people who are often left on the margins of sport.You use AI every day. articles.title: In a Croatian road test, wood ash boosted weak clay’s load-bearing capacity by up to 235%; it rose another 31%-39% in just 14 days
articles.summary: A groundbreaking Croatian study reveals that wood ash can significantly enhance the load-bearing capacity of weak clay roads by up to 235%, with ongoing strength improvements even after construction.
articles.body: Roads built on clay have a familiar weakness. When the soil is wet, it softens and a soft subgrade cannot carry the loads that the layers above it pass down. The usual remedies are to add binders such as lime or cement, or to bring in gravel and sand and each of these has a cost, especially where good stone is scarce and transport makes up a large share of the bill. A possible source of help is biomass plants and wood-processing factories. Wood combustion results in ash, which is generally dumped in a landfill. The ash contains calcium that reacts and hardens over time, which raises a question for road builders whether a waste product can replace a purchased binder or imported aggregate.The Strizivojna Hrast test section, built in 2023Sanja Dimter, Goran Kuburić, Ernest Ević and Goran Vrhovac tested that question in Road building using wood ash, published in the December 2024 issue of Građevinar. The experiment took place on an internal road at the Strizivojna Hrast factory, which makes parquet and other wood products, in Strizivojna, Osijek-Baranja County. The factory had a cogeneration plant that burned about 110 tonnes of wood biomass per day, and the ash accumulated in a landfill next to the plant. Eight to ten heavy trucks with log trailers, weighing 36 to 40 tonnes, travelled the access roads daily.Bearing capacity rose 155% to 235% on a 50:50 clay and wood ash subgradeThe test section, 80 square metres in total, was built in two fields, the first in June 2023 and the second in September 2023. The first field placed the pavement on the natural subgrade and the second placed it on an ash-stabilised subgrade. The soil consisted of medium-plasticity clay with a laboratory California Bearing Ratio of 2%. In the field, the natural subgrade had a compressive modulus of 12 MN/m², well below the 30 MN/m² minimum in Croatia’s general technical conditions for road works, as cited by the authors. Factory employees mixed the excavated clay with the wood ash mixture from the landfill in equal parts, then compacted it in a layer 15 to 17 cm thick. According to the abstract, this increased the subgrade’s bearing capacity by 155% to 235% compared with natural clay. That is roughly 2.6 to 3.4 times the bearing capacity of the natural clay.In laboratory tests, a 50:50 mixture of clay and wood ash reached a California Bearing Ratio (CBR) of 9%, compared with 2% for untreated clay, which the authors describe as a 350% increase. This is a different measure from the field figures above. The authors’ conclusions describe the subgrade as reaching up to four times the bearing capacity of natural clay, which appears to reflect the highest field reading (48.4 MN/m² against 12 MN/m²) and not the 155% to 235% range in the abstract.A further 31% to 39% gain after 14 daysThe team tested the subgrade on 20 September and again on 3 October 2023. The abstract reports that its bearing capacity rose by 31% to 39% within 14 days of construction, as the wood ash continued to bind the soil. The paper’s table shows more variation. Five points gained between 11% and 57%, while a sixth point, in a wet area, fell from 48.4 to 36.1 MN/m² but still met the 30 MN/m² minimum. The authors attributed the gain to the binding properties of the ash. Calcium oxide made up 33.38% to 46.9% of the ash by mass, depending on the fraction. The 50:50 mixture reached a compressive strength of 0.48 MN/m² after seven days and 0.55 MN/m² after 28 days, above the Croatian minimums for lime-stabilised mixtures of 0.40 MN/m² at seven days and 0.50 MN/m² at 28 days.A 2022 laboratory study on replacing part of the lime A separate study approached the material in the laboratory. Martina Zagvozda, Tatjana Rukavina and Sanja Dimter tested wood ash as a partial replacement for lime in Wood bioash effect as lime replacement in the stabilisation of different clay subgrades, published in the International Journal of Pavement Engineering. The authors found that the best blend depended on soil plasticity. High-plasticity clays tolerated only 25% to 50% replacement of lime, while medium- and low-plasticity soils could take 50% to 75% and still match or beat the reference mixture in CBR.Across all mixtures, CBR ranged from 18.82% to 107.34%, and linear swelling dropped below 1%. The authors cautioned, however, that some aspects of wood-ash chemistry may limit wider use.A wood ash base course remeasured in June 2024Both fields used an ash base layer covered by a 10 cm layer of crushed stone. The ash base reached compressive moduli of 60 to 80 MN/m², the same range the paper reports for the sand base layers commonly used in Slavonia and Baranja. Heavy trucks used the road daily after construction. In June 2024, one year after the first field was built, the authors remeasured the traffic surface and found compressive moduli of 75 to 85 MN/m², with no deformation or damage observed. The paper, published in December 2024, reported no later measurements.What one 80-square-metre test section does and does not establishThe above-mentioned study was a preliminary note covering only a small area of private factory road. The 50% ash content was chosen for practical reasons, not from a laboratory mix design and the authors said better results could be expected with further testing at different ash contents. The authors did not analyse current material prices, so the case for cost savings rests on wood ash being free of charge. Taken together, the two studies support a balanced conclusion. Locally produced wood ash stiffened poor clay soils in eastern Croatia and performed comparably to sand as a base course under heavy trucks. Whether the same holds on public roads, and with other clays and other wood ashes, remains to be shown.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A rare I.M. Pei-designed Texas mansion goes on sale for $22 million for the first time since 1969; the 19,133-square-foot estate has three kitchens, two wine cellars and a glass-roofed garden room
articles.summary: A unique Fort Worth estate in Texas, designed by I.M. Pei, has hit the market for $22 million.
articles.body: A unique Fort Worth estate in Texas, designed by I.M. Pei, has hit the market for $22 million. This is the first time the landmark property in Westover Hills has been offered for sale since it was constructed in 1969, according to Realtor.com. The property is listed by Madeline Jobst, Ralph Randall and Ashley Mooring of Briggs Freeman Sotheby's International Realty.One of only three private residences designed by I.M. PeiThe 19,133-square-foot mansion in Westover Hills is one of only three private homes designed by the late Chinese-American architect I.M. Pei during his lifetime. Westover House is “the last and the greatest”, according to the listing on Sotheby's. “It is one of the most significant achievements in American residential architecture.” The house reflects the design style of Pritzker Prize winner Pei’s famous works, including the Louvre Pyramid in Paris and the East Building of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.The sprawling home sits on nearly four acres atop a hill in Fort Worth’s exclusive Westover Hills neighbourhood. Pei, known for his modernist style, designed marvellous structures across the globe, but private homes were rare for him. The architect died in 2019 at the age of 102. His Texas work also includes the Morton H. Meyerson Symphony Center in Dallas, which many people in the region know well. The Fort Worth house follows the same approach, with clean lines, concrete walls and large windows that bring the outdoors inside.Westover House was built as a family homeWestover House was built for Anne Burnett Tandy, an oil heiress, and her husband, Charles Tandy. Charles led a company that started as a leather goods business and grew into a large retail operation. It later acquired RadioShack. Charles Tandy died in 1978, and Anne passed away two years later. The home was then passed to their daughter, Anne Marion, who lived there until her death in 2020. The Tandy family still owns the property, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.Inside the houseBuilt in 1969, the house spans 19,133 sq ft and features a unique layout with museum-inspired interiors, a soaring glass-roofed garden room, an art gallery, a luxurious primary suite and a wellness retreat.“At the heart of Westover House is the garden room: a soaring, light-filled space. Its canted roof of glass and steel rises above the tree line, and Pei carried its triangular geometry throughout the house, repeating the slope in four smaller angled peaks that serve as ‘light grabbers’ – north-facing glass panels that pull natural light deep into the living spaces from morning through dusk,” the listing says.The single-storey home has seven bedrooms and three kitchens. Its thick concrete walls are made with rose-quartz granite from Colorado, with all the textured lines carved by hand. Portuguese marble and Burmese teak flooring run throughout the rooms. The outdoor terraces are finished in granite.There are two formal living areas and two formal dining areas on either side of the garden room. Each has a large and a small room connected to one another, making the spaces ideal for entertaining.The art gallery is a spacious hall off the garden room that connects to the private part of the house. The primary suite features a large bedroom with a sitting area, a study area, a private bathroom and ample closet space. It also has a library, a fireplace and a wet bar, along with an adjoining second bedroom with its own bathroom and a large closet.There are two additional bedrooms and bathrooms in the guest quarters. The house also has a cocktail bar, three fireplaces, a den, an office/study in the private wing, a wellness room and an elevator. The large basement houses two climate-controlled wine cellars, while a separate laundry room and a staff area with two bathrooms complete the home.Outside, the 3.86-acre lot includes a heated pool, a putting green and a six-car garage with a carport for four cars.According to the listing, Westover House is more than an architectural triumph. “It is a Fort Worth legend.” Interior designers including Melanie Kahane, Benjamin Baldwin, Ron Bradshaw, Valliant Interiors and Windfohr Design have worked on the house.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Barbra Streisand donated $10 million to Cedars-Sinai’s women’s heart center; in 2026, the center bearing her name is leading a new $7.5 million NIH-funded five-year study on women’s aging
articles.summary: Aging is rarely a single-system story. The heart, brain, muscles and blood vessels change together, yet medical research has often studied them separately.
articles.body: Aging is rarely a single-system story. The heart, brain, muscles and blood vessels change together, yet medical research has often studied them separately. A new five-year research project at Cedars-Sinai is taking a broader view, investigating whether damage to the body’s smallest blood vessels could help explain several health challenges women face as they grow older.Backed by a $7.5 million grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the National Institute on Aging (NIA), the study brings together specialists in cardiovascular health, neurology, biostatistics and frailty research. At its centre is a question with implications far beyond cardiology: could understanding tiny blood vessels reveal new ways to protect the ageing heart, brain and body?Looking beyond the heartThe research is being led by investigators at the Smidt Heart Institute’s Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center, named after the legendary singer and actor following her $10 million donation to Cedars-Sinai.The new initiative, known as the Microvascular Aging Effects—Women’s Evaluation of Systemic Aging Tenacity in Heart, Brain and Frailty study, or MAE-WEST HBF, has been established as a Specialized Center of Research Excellence on Sex Differences through the NIH Office of Research on Women’s Health. Its focus is the microvasculature: the network of tiny blood vessels that delivers oxygen and nutrients throughout the body. Researchers want to understand how deterioration in these vessels may connect not only to cardiovascular disease but also to cognitive decline and reduced physical strength.A trail of cluesThe project builds on years of work at Cedars-Sinai examining coronary microvascular disease, a condition that affects the smallest blood vessels supplying the heart and is more common in women.Previous research from the Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center has linked small-vessel disease, chronic inflammation and iron accumulation with impaired function in the heart, brain and kidneys, alongside declining physical strength.That history gives the new study a strong foundation. Rather than examining individual conditions in isolation, researchers will explore whether they share underlying biological pathways.The distinction is important because women can experience cardiovascular symptoms that are less obvious than the classic signs associated with heart disease. Microvascular disease has historically been overlooked or mistaken for other conditions, leaving some patients without appropriate diagnosis or treatment.Connecting heart, brain and mobilityMAE-WEST HBF brings together a multidisciplinary team to investigate what happens beyond the cardiovascular system. Neurology researchers at Cedars-Sinai will examine the relationship between small-vessel damage and brain health, while collaborators at UCLA will handle biostatistical analysis. Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington will focus on frailty and physical function.The ambition is to understand whether a problem in the smallest vessels can set off a wider chain of age-related changes.If researchers can establish those connections, the findings could eventually influence how doctors screen for risk and identify people who may be vulnerable to several conditions at once.Rethinking healthy ageingWomen generally live longer than men, but longevity does not necessarily mean more years in good health. Women also experience higher rates of chronic illness, meaning a longer lifespan can include more time living with disability or declining function.That makes prevention particularly important. The researchers envision a future where healthy ageing involves earlier screening, better imaging and more personalised preventive care, identifying biological risks before they develop into major disease.The study also reflects a broader shift in women's health research: moving away from treating individual organs as separate systems and towards understanding how the body ages as a whole.After decades of research into women's cardiovascular health, the latest initiative aims to connect three crucial measures of wellbeing healthy heart, a functioning brain and the ability to remain physically strong and independent.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and istockYou use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis on Sunday hit back at former chief minister Uddhav Thackeray for backing calls for a “regime
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis on Sunday hit back at former chief minister Uddhav Thackeray for backing calls for a “regime change” in India, saying the Shiv Sena (UBT) president had failed to prevent a regime change within his own party.Also Read | ‘Taking away right to vote, protest’: Uddhav backs opposition's ‘regime change’ call against government“First of all, Uddhav Thackeray could not prevent a regime change within his own Shiv Sena, so I do not know what other regime change he is talking about. The moment his party abandoned Hindutva and the ideology of Hindu Hriday Samrat Balasaheb Thackeray, such turmoil erupted within the party that those who wanted to follow Balasaheb Thackeray’s principles formed the real Shiv Sena,” Fadnavis told reporters in Nagpur.Fadnavis was referring to the June 2022 split in the undivided Shiv Sena, which led to the formation of two factions led by Uddhav Thackeray and Maharashtra deputy chief Minister Eknath Shinde.The chief minister asserted that any regime change in India could take place only through elections, not through street protests.“I have made it very clear: Stop fighting against the Constitution of India. Decisions in this country will be taken in Parliament and in accordance with the Constitution, not on the streets. In a democracy, governments are decided through elections,” he said.Fadnavis expressed confidence that Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government would return to power in 2029 and called on the opposition to win public support to secure an electoral victory.“Today, Narendra Modi’s government is in power, and it will be elected again. But if you want a regime change, you must contest elections, win the hearts of the people and secure an electoral victory. Those who dream of bringing about a regime change in India by disregarding the Constitution, as witnessed in Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan, will never succeed in their intentions,” the chief minister added, referring to the youth- and student-led movements that toppled incumbent governments in three of India’s neighbouring countries in recent years.Fadnavis’ comments came a day after Uddhav Thackeray backed recent calls by activists and opposition leaders for a regime change in India, arguing that denying people the right to express their views through elections and protests would leave them with no option but to seek a change of government.“If you take away our right to express our views through elections and protest, then we're standing up just to overthrow this government,” the Shiv Sena (UBT) chief said.The remarks come amid a political row over references to regime change by opposition leaders and student activists during ongoing protests in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Senior advocate Prashant Bhushan, student activist and All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora, and Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera have publicly used or discussed the phrase “regime change” at conferences and press briefings in connection with the protests.(with ANI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: At Louisiana’s Fort Polk, researchers spread pulverized classified paper on damaged Army land; native plant cover was 48% higher at one soil site and 42% higher at another
articles.summary: Researchers at Fort Polk, Louisiana, find that pulverized classified paper boosts native plant growth by 45% on military training lands, offering a sustainable solution for soil rehabilitation.
articles.body: Researchers at Fort Polk, Louisiana, investigated whether pulverised classified paper waste could help restore military training land. Military training grounds can experience soil disturbance from movement of vehicles and soldiers across the land, making vegetation establishment more difficult. The US Agricultural Research Service (ARS) reported that native plant cover was 45% higher on plots receiving the recommended paper treatment compared to control plots. The experiment examined whether shredded paper could serve as a soil amendment while providing an alternative use for waste otherwise sent to landfill. The findings were published in 2019 in Soil and Tillage Research, wherein researchers recommended applying pulverised paper at 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare.How researchers tested the paper amendmentThe field experiment began in April 2015, when researchers spread pulverised paper obtained from document-shredding facilities across experimental plots and incorporated it into the upper 15 centimetres of soil. They then planted four native warm-season grasses: big bluestem, Indiangrass, little bluestem and switchgrass.The experiment used two soil types; the first was an Alfisol, taken from more fertile soil conditions at one site, while the second was an Ultisol, which had lower fertility. Different quantities of paper were then applied at each location, and the results were compared to untreated control plots and plots that were treated with conventional soil.The rates differed because the researchers encountered difficulties incorporating the highest application levels into the Alfisol soil. The Ultisol plots received rates of 17.9, 35.9, 53.8 and 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare, and the rates at the Alfisol site were 9.0, 17.9, 26.9 and 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare. Consequently, 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare was the highest rate tested at the Ultisol site.The conventional treatment consisted of lime, applied at 2,240 kilograms per hectare, and nitrogen fertiliser at 56 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare. The control plots received neither amendment nor fertiliser, although they were prepared and seeded in the same way as the other plots.Different soil conditions produced different resultsThe scientific paper provides the site-specific figures behind the findings, and at the Alfisol site, native plant cover at 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare was 48% higher than the control and 62% higher than the conventional treatment. Conversely, at the Ultisol site, native plant cover at 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare, the highest rate tested there, was 42% higher than the control and 17% higher than the conventional treatment.In terms of plant cover and plant biomass, different results were also produced. At the Ultisol site, native plant biomass at 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare was 71% lower than the control, while the conventional treatment produced 355% more. At the Alfisol site, native plant biomass at 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare was 90% higher than the control and 96% higher than the conventional treatment. These measurements indicate that greater plant cover did not necessarily mean greater plant biomass across both sites.The researchers linked the contrasting responses to differences in nutrient availability. The Ultisol site showed improvements in certain physical and chemical soil properties, but its low fertility meant that nitrogen immobilisation could constrain grass growth. At the more fertile Alfisol site, the carbon-rich paper tied up nitrogen, which helped reduce competition from weeds and invasive plants and favoured the planted native grasses. ARS also reported estimated savings of about $11,600 per hectare and annual savings of around $20,000 per military facility, alongside a potential diversion of about 64 metric tonnes of paper from landfill. Subsequently, the Corps of Engineers produced a user guide based on the research to help military facilities consider the approach to land rehabilitation.You use AI every day. articles.title: What help can Egypt offer Saudi Arabia in the war against the Houthis?
articles.summary: Analysts say that any move from Egypt will remain ‘strictly defensive’, as the conflict in Yemen intensifies.
articles.body:
Egypt’s parliament is convening on Sunday after President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi requested an emergency session to approve defensive military aid to Saudi Arabia, if Riyadh asks for support in its war with Yemen’s Houthis.

The request comes as the Iran-backed armed group continues attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the capital, Riyadh, and its airports and oil facilities.

El-Sisi declared that Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia, in a speech on Saturday, but said that he “hopes” the parliament will give him authorisation to proceed.

On Sunday, Egypt said it would provide “all necessary and possible support to Saudi Arabia to defend its safety and stability”. The National Defence Council, chaired by President el-Sisi, said it “stands fully with” Saudi Arabia to defend its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites.

But what would Egyptian assistance look like? And what capacity does it have to “protect” Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis?

What’s behind el-Sisi’s decision to offer help to Saudi Arabia?

Saudi Arabia has long been a strategic and economic partner of Egypt, and el-Sisi said in a statement last month that Saudi security is “integral” to Egypt’s security.

Political analyst and Gulf studies expert Thomas Bonnie James told Al Jazeera that the Houthi security threat to the kingdom is one of the “converging” pressures that have led to this decision. The other one, is economics.

“Houthi pressure on [Bab] al-Mandeb threatens the Suez Canal , which Egypt’s foreign minister says has lost about $11bn since the attacks began in 2023,” he said, referring to Houthi attacks on Israeli-linked ships passing through the narrow strait, carried out in solidarity with Gaza.

James suggested that the decision is also important to Cairo, because “millions of Egyptians live and work in Saudi Arabia, which is Egypt’s largest single source of remittances. An Egyptian resident was killed, and others were injured in the attacks on Riyadh’s airport.”

He also said that Egypt does not want to be seen as the regional ally that “stood aside while others defended the kingdom,” as Turkiye and Pakistan have made their own pledges after activating the Mecca defence pact signed in August amid the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East.

Hostilities in Yemen continue to escalate. Two air raids by the Saudi-led coalition hit Hodeidah in the southwest on Sunday.

Saudi forces also intercepted drones near Riyadh and Eastern provinces. The capital’s King Khalid international airport has come under attack at least 20 times since fighting flared between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God.

The Saudi-backed forces are fighting the Houthis on several fronts, including Taiz and Marib, and some analysts argue the Houthis are stretched thin after their summer gains.

But James told Al Jazeera “that defeating them outright is a tall order”.

“Ground forces backed by air power can retake the coastline; stopping missiles launched from the mountains is much harder,” he said.

When will the Egyptian parliament convene?

They will be convening on Sunday at 1pm local time (10am GMT).

Under the Egyptian law, the President cannot declare war or send the military on foreign missions without the approval from the parliament.

For the authorisation to be granted, at least two-thirds of the politicians in the House of Representatives must vote in favour of the proposal.

Does Egypt have security cooperation with Saudi Arabia?

Not exactly. Egypt and Saudi Arabia have not signed a formal bilateral or multilateral pact on defence cooperation. But Cairo has a long history of cooperation with Riyadh.

Egypt is a founding member of the Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition, which Saudi Arabia launched in July. It aims to protect shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb – territories on Yemen’s coastline. Houthis captured towns and cities near Bab al-Mandeb last month, but the internationally recognised government has since wrested control of some of the areas from the Iran-backed group.

Egypt also participated in joint military exercises with Saudi Arabia in 2024.

Cairo was also part of a 2015 coalition , cobled together after the Houthi group captured large areas of north and western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa in September 2024. Egypt contributed naval and air forces to help secure maritime corridors in the Red Sea against the Houthis.

But James, the Gulf studies expert, told Al Jazeera that what el-Sisi is proposing is different from the maritime defence coalition Egypt recently joined.

“He is hoping for authorisation to deploy Egyptian forces to help defend Saudi territory itself,” he said. “It would move Egypt from a multilateral maritime framework to a bilateral military commitment.”

What will be the nature of Egyptian assistance to Saudi Arabia?

El-Sisi explicitly said that he is only proposing “defence” and that he isn’t “speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone”.

Military Defence Analyst Alexandru Hudisteanu said that the use of counter-drones and anti-missile support is a high probability if the decision is authorised.

“It would be the most urgent need at this point to make sure that the defence of Saudi Arabia is backed up and reinforced,” he told Al Jazeera.

Simultaneously, he added that the request itself is also a strategic move of deterrence.

“We know Saudi Arabia has one of the most prolific militaries out there in terms of capacities and capabilities. It’s a matter of the territory which Saudi Arabia needs to cover at any given moment,” Hudisteanu said.

James said that any contribution by Egypt would focus on the protection of Saudi territory, using “air and missile defence around critical infrastructure, intercepting drones, naval escort and intelligence sharing”.

James said that it is unlikely Egypt will deploy troops to Yemen’s front lines.

In the 1960s, former Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser deployed tens of thousands of troops in the Yemen Civil War. Saudi Arabia backed the rival side. Egypt suffered heavy casualties and Saudi-Egyptian ties were strained.

“What Egypt will not want is to send troops into Yemen. Nasser’s intervention there in the 1960s sends a clear message: defend the kingdom, don’t take ownership of Yemen,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: At Fort Campbell, Tennessee, researchers mixed processed household trash into soil; the highest dose helped native prairie grasses establish better than on control plots
articles.summary: Discover how researchers at Fort Campbell, Tennessee, found that incorporating processed household waste into soil significantly improved native prairie grass establishment, with implications for land restoration efforts.
articles.body: Fort Campbell is a military installation in Tennessee, where it was found that native prairie grasses grew more successfully in plots that were treated with high doses of a processed household-waste by-product. Researchers recorded significantly greater native-grass cover in the highest-dose plots than in untreated controls, during a two-growing-season study.Can organic material help in restoring disturbed land? The project tried to answer this by sterilising household waste and separating its organic and inorganic components, with researchers incorporating the uncomposted organic by-product into silt loam soil before sowing native prairie grasses.Researchers tested five application ratesThe team applied the material at rates of zero, 4.5, 9, 18 and 36 metric tonnes per hectare, and the plots were seeded with native prairie grasses and were monitored over two growing seasons. The researchers were able to compare the treatments with natural vegetation recovery with the help of an additional unseeded control. The highest application rate produced a lot more native-grass basal cover and a greater share of native grasses in the plant community than the controls. Basal cover measures the area that has been occupied by plants at the soil surface, while percentage composition is an indicator of how much of the vegetation consists of the target grasses.Accumulation of plant phosphorus also increased as the application rate rose; phosphorus is an important plant nutrient, and the measurements suggested that the processed material supplied nutrients that the grasses could use. The experiment showed that the greatest improvement in native-grass establishment occurred at the highest rate tested, 36 metric tonnes per hectare.The material changed soil nutrient levelsWhen it came to soil chemistry, phosphorus and lead concentrations increased in the upper 10 centimetres of soil at the highest application rates where the material had been mixed in. The authors reported few environmental effects during the trial and concluded that the material improved the establishment of perennial grass and plant nutrition at the highest rate. It is important to note that the study does not infer that every processed household-waste product would be suitable for every restoration site, or that the same application rate would be safe under all soil conditions. The research was published in Communications in Soil Science and Plant Analysis in 2010, and its authors included researchers from the US Army Engineer Research and Development Center, the US Department of Agriculture’s Agricultural Research Service and the University of Illinois.A related study tested the material on degraded landThe same type of waste-processing by-product was examined in a separate study at Fort Benning in Georgia, which was published in the Journal of Plant Nutrition in 2007. It tested the material on moderately and highly degraded sandy loam soils over two growing seasons, where material at rates of zero, 18, 36, 72, and 143 metric tonnes per hectare were applied. They found improvements in available nutrients and soil pH at both sites, and the treatment also reduced soil bulk density and increased soil carbon and nitrogen concentrations. The study’s results provide related evidence for using processed organic waste in land restoration, but the sites, soil conditions, and application rates were different from those at Fort Campbell.The results depend on the site and doseThe Fort Campbell trial found that processed household waste could help native grasses establish on disturbed land, particularly at the highest rate tested, but also cautioned that the results could not be universally applied. The increase in soil lead and phosphorus also means that any wider use would require testing of the material and the receiving soil, as researchers would need to consider nutrient needs, soil chemistry, and the possibility of contaminants accumulating before applying the approach at other sites. The study supports further investigation of processed organic waste as a soil amendment, and its findings are specific to the product, site, and conditions tested over two growing seasons.You use AI every day. articles.title: Funeral held for 75 Palestinians after remains recovered from Gaza ruins
articles.summary: Most of the victims were from the Daraj neighbourhood in Gaza City, the Health Ministry says.
articles.body:
A mass funeral has been held for 75 Palestinians whose remains were found recently under the rubble of homes and buildings destroyed in the months since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, the Ministry of Health announced.

Hundreds of Palestinians attended the funeral procession before the remains were buried at the Sheikh Radwan Cemetery on Sunday morning.

Most of the victims were from the Daraj neighbourhood in the northeastern part of Gaza City.

Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Khaled said the majority of the remains belonged to women and children “who were inside their homes when they were targeted”.

The remains consisted of some body parts and personal belongings and were wrapped in Palestinian flags before the burial, she said.

Abdullah al-Majdalawi, director of public relations and media for Gaza’s Civil Defence, told the Turkish state news agency Anadolu that the remains had been recovered over recent weeks from several destroyed homes in Daraj.

He said the buildings were bombed while residents were inside during the early months of the war and that the victims belonged to about 20 Palestinian families, including people who had been displaced to the homes.

Efforts to recover bodies from beneath the rubble continue to face severe difficulties due to a lack of equipment and heavy machinery, he added.

The Civil Defence launched the second phase of its recovery operations in July. It recovered 333 bodies and remains of 559 people during its first operation in November 2025.

The Civil Defence says it believes the remains of another 8,000 Palestinians are still trapped beneath the rubble across Gaza. There are about 200,000 damaged and destroyed buildings in Gaza, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.

At least 74,475 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched the genocidal war three years ago.

articles.title: In 2010, artists began turning a vacant Houston lot into a park using broken dishes, bottle caps, shells, keys and discarded tiles; 16 years later, more than 300 artists have filled it with a 400-foot mosaic wall and free public art
articles.summary: What began as an abandoned patch of land in southeast Houston has slowly transformed into something far more magical: a public park assembled from the
articles.body: What began as an abandoned patch of land in southeast Houston has slowly transformed into something far more magical: a public park assembled from the fragments of everyday life. Broken crockery, discarded tiles, shells, bottle caps, keys and scraps of found objects have found new purpose here, brought together by hundreds of artists into a sprawling celebration of colour, memory and imagination.Sixteen years after work began, Smither Park has become a living example of what can happen when discarded materials are given another chance, states an October 2016 report by the Houston Chronicle.From vacant lot to visual wonderAccording to the online report, before artists arrived, the half-acre site on Munger Street was little more than an eyesore. The land, already owned by the Orange Show Center for Visionary Art, was chosen for a new park dedicated to the memory of John Smither, a collector and supporter of outsider art.His wife, Stephanie Smither, a longtime Orange Show board member, wanted the space to honour his legacy. The project found an ideal creative partner in builder and artist Dan Phillips, whose work frequently incorporates reclaimed and discarded materials, adds the report.Construction began in 2010, with the foundations of what would become the park's signature feature: a 400-foot mosaic memory wall.A wall made of memoriesAs per the report, the wall is less a conventional piece of public art than a giant collage assembled from thousands of fragments. Bathroom tiles sit alongside nail polish bottles, shells, clay figures, broken dishes and other salvaged objects.Across its length, the colourful surface forms animals, abstract patterns and playful figures. More than 300 artists have contributed to the project over the years, turning individual pieces of material into a collective artwork.The result feels deliberately eclectic and nothing appears too precious or perfectly matched. Instead, the charm comes from the unexpected combinations and the sense that almost anything can become part of the composition.Whimsy at every turnAccording to the report, the mosaic wall is only the beginning. Over the years, the park has grown to include a pavilion decorated with recycled glass bottles, a fish-themed band shell, a swing set, a meditation garden and a marble tower.The tower is among the park's more interactive attractions, designed around the simple pleasure of watching a marble travel through an elaborate sequence of cups, saucers, roasting pans and fan blades. Its playful mechanics fit naturally into a space where art is meant to be touched, explored and experienced rather than simply observed.The park's various structures each have their own visual language, yet the use of recycled and donated materials ties everything together.Art without a price tagThe report claims that the project was completed for around $1.2 million, largely through private donations. Many of the artists contributed their time without payment, while much of the material was donated, recycled or rescued from being discarded. That approach is central to Smither Park's character. Its raw materials are not hidden behind polished finishes. Their previous lives remain visible, giving the work an unusual sense of history.Even after the park's formal opening, the creative process has continued. Artists still visit the materials warehouse, sorting through boxes of fragments in search of something that might complete their next idea.A portrait of HoustonMore than a collection of colourful objects, Smither Park has become a portrait of its city and its people. Its mixture of cultures, materials, ideas and artistic styles reflects a place that is constantly being rebuilt and reimagined.The park's greatest achievement may be the way it turns the overlooked into the unforgettable. A broken dish becomes part of a wall; a discarded bottle becomes a detail in a pavilion; an empty lot becomes a gathering place.Images Courtesy: Houston ChronicleYou use AI every day. articles.title: Pope Leo welcomed back as he delivers Angelus prayer days after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Thousands gathered in St. Peter's Square as Pope Leo XIV made a surprise early return from Gemelli hospital following cancerous tumor removal.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV made a remarkable return to the Vatican on Sunday, appearing before thousands of Catholic faithful in St. Peter's Square just five days after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung. The 71-year-old pontiff delivered his traditional Angelus prayer from a window overlooking the square, marking his first official engagement since being discharged Saturday from Rome's Gemelli hospital, where doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung. Leo thanked the faithful for their prayers and support throughout his hospitalization, saying his recent health struggles had brought him closer to those suffering from illness. He also expressed gratitude to the doctors, nurses and hospital staff who cared for him following the operation. POPE LEO XIV DISCHARGED FROM HOSPITAL, WILL RETURN TO VATICAN AFTER SURGERY TO REMOVE LUNG CANCER The first American-born pope said he planned to gradually resume his regular activities with God's help and the continued prayers of the faithful. During his Angelus address, Leo reflected on one of Jesus' best-known teachings, "Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's," urging Christians to live with integrity and resist hypocrisy. His return came sooner than expected after doctors initially anticipated a hospital stay of approximately one week following Tuesday's surgery. As he departed the hospital on Saturday, the pope told a reporter in English that he was doing "much better." Claire Holland, visiting from Jacksonville, Fla., told The Associated Press she felt "very blessed" to witness the pope's return. "I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said. POPE LEO UNDERGOES BLOOD TESTS, X-RAY FOLLOWING CANCER SURGERY, VATICAN SAYS The surgery marked the first major health crisis of Leo's 17-month pontificate. Doctors confirmed that the tumor was adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Doctors are conducting further testing on the tumor and surrounding lymph nodes to determine the extent of the disease and whether additional treatment, including chemotherapy, immunotherapy or targeted therapy, may be necessary. The pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 through Nov. 17, a demanding itinerary that includes a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high-altitude destinations. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that the pope appears well enough to go on the trip. "The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora said, adding that he expected Leo to recover fully from the surgery "in another 10 days or so." articles.title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
articles.summary: At least one person was killed in the strikes, which also hit a data centre used by Russia's equivalent of Facebook.
articles.body:
At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.

The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.

A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.

Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.

Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.

It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.

Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July .

Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.

St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.

He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.

Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.

Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire.

It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".

As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.

Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism , including from some US Republicans.

However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps.

Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.

Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.

Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.

Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

articles.title: Forget New York and Chicago: An unlikely American city is becoming a pizza lover's paradise
articles.summary: A small Connecticut city is proving it belongs alongside New York City in the pizza world, with apizza tours, white clam pies and a pizza-themed hotel suite.
articles.body: New York City and Chicago may be the American cities best known for their pizza, but another city — in Connecticut, of all places — has carved out its own slice of the pie. In New Haven, pizza fans can now bike between famous pizzerias, sleep in a pizza-themed hotel suite and even visit a museum exhibit devoted to the city's signature food. Just in time for National Pizza Month, historian and self-described "pizza guru" Colin Caplan has launched a new pizza crawl aboard the Elm City Party Bike, a 15-passenger pedal-powered trolley. AMERICA' S BEST PIZZERIAS CROWNED IN NEW RANKINGS AS PIZZA EXPERT SHARES SKEPTICISM The bike has operated in the city for the past nine years. Now,for the first time, it's being used specifically for pizza tours. Guests can choose their own pizzerias or take a guided tour with Caplan — who is also a professional tour guide, author, architect and founder of Taste New Haven — sampling similar pies from several restaurants and comparing them. "We're going to try cheese pizza from three or four different places, and then we'll rate it at the end, and you can decide what's better," Caplan told Fox News Digital. "It's a great way to team build, to have the pizza together, to be outside, to frolic and have some fun." AMERICA'S MOST AND LEAST EXPENSIVE PLACES TO ORDER PIZZA REVEALED IN NEW STUDY The rolling pizza party is just one example of how deeply the dish has become woven into New Haven's identity. The Omni New Haven Hotel at Yale even offers a Pizza Suite decorated with the city's signature food, along with gift cards to famed New Haven pizzerias Sally's Apizza and Frank Pepe Pizzeria Napoletana — two of the spots that make up the so-called "Holy Trinity" of New Haven-style apizza; the third is Modern Apizza. Visitors build entire trips around the city's pie, Caplan said. "We actually have people who are doing staycations from all over the country," he added. PHILADELPHIA PIZZA SHOP SELLS $55 SLICES TOPPED WITH CAVIAR, SERVED ON GOLD PLATE WITH KEEPSAKE SPOON New Haven has increasingly earned a place alongside America's better-known pizza destinations, Caplan said, set apart by its signature style, which is locally known as "apizza." It features a thin, crispy, chewy and slightly charred crust. "Let's face it, New York City has always been the center of pizza in everyone's mind," Caplan said, noting Chicago and Detroit as runners-up. "Everyone knows about these big cities and the pizza scene. What New Haven has had to do was prove itself." A traditional pie in New Haven can be remarkably simple, he said, topped only with tomato sauce and some grated Pecorino Romano. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "People are obsessed with cheese," Caplan said. "But, I want to tell you something. The real pizza, the original pizzas — they didn't have tons of cheese." In addition to its more traditional approach to cheese, the city is also known for its white clam pizza, famously associated with Frank Pepe. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Caplan's go-to topping, however, has an unexpectedly salty twist: anchovies. "That little brininess, that little bit of salt, that extra protein, that flavor — it is, to me, complete," he said. Anchovy-topped pizza was also the original option in New Haven for diners who wanted something other than a plain pie, he said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Those traditions are part of what Caplan believes makes New Haven's pizza culture worth traveling for, and it's about more than just determining which city has the best pies. "People are coming for pizza, but they're seeing the culture. They're seeing what we really have here," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "For a small city, we pack a big punch."

articles.title: WATCH: Virginia cops crawl through burning house to save man trapped in fire
articles.summary: Body-worn camera footage captures four Culpeper, Virginia, police officers crawling through heavy smoke to drag an unresponsive man to safety.
articles.body: As police officers raced up to a wooden house in the town of Culpeper, Virginia on the evening of Oct. 3, heavy smoke billowed out of the windows. Residents who lived in separate apartments in the house stood outside, according to the Culpeper Police Department. But one man hadn’t come out, they told police. They worried that he might be inside. MYSTERY STRANGER VANISHES AFTER FAMILY SAYS FRANTIC WARNING SAVED THEIR LIVES DURING DEVASTATING HOUSE FIRE Officer Ashley Sain didn’t wait. She rushed toward the house and went in without protective gear and began checking doors, searching for anyone who might still be inside. Moments later, Officer Neal Coffey joined her. SHERIFF'S DEPUTY SAVES MAN FROM FIERY WRECK AFTER HIGH-SPEED CHASE ENDS IN CRASH Body-worn camera footage shows one officer running up stairs, past "No Smoking" signs with red lettering posted on the walls. On the second floor, the duo found a door that was locked from the inside. Smoke slipped through through cracks above and below. MARINE VETERAN AND BOSTON FIREFIGHTER DIES AFTER RESCUE EFFORTS AT MASSIVE HOUSE BLAZE "Police department, if you’re in here!" Sain shouted over shrieking smoke alarms. Meanwhile, Coffey quickly opened the lock with a pocket-size tool and cautiously swung open the door, calling out, "Police department!" HISTORIC NYC CHURCH ENGULFED IN 5-ALARM BLAZE; 6 FIREFIGHTERS INJURED BATTLING STUBBORN FLAMES But there was no answer. Heavy black smoke poured from the bedroom. The officers could see flames. MASSIVE FIRE ENGULFS APARTMENT COMPLEX UNDER CONSTRUCTION, FORCES EVACUATIONS IN SOUTH BEND "Police department!" Sain shouted again. "Anybody inside?" By that time, Sgt. David Cole and Officer Michael Beel had made it to the second floor, as well. HEART-STOPPING VIDEO SHOWS OFFICERS USE UNLIKELY TOOL TO SAVE FAMILY TRAPPED IN FLOODWATERS Body-worn camera footage shows Coffey crawling on his hands and knees, then flat on the wooden plank floor, searching the room with a flashlight. "I can’t see!" he shouted with a tone of increasing desperation, as he pushed through thicker smoke. POLICE DOG FOLLOWS HIS NOSE TO FIND MISSING AUTISTIC TEEN SCREAMING FOR HELP He inched forward on his chest, feeling around through the smoke. Suddenly, he found a man lying unresponsive on a bed. "Hey brother, come on!" he urges frantically, tugging the man’s arm. FIREFIGHTERS, POLICE PULL YOUNG WOMAN FROM SEWAGE-FILLED RAVINE AFTER DAYS TRAPPED IN 104-DEGREE HEAT "Come on! Come with me!" He shouted again through the smoke to fellow officers. "We’ve got to get him out! I have him! He’s breathing!" Video shows him struggling to move the man. "Hey! We need help!" an officer shouted. Coffey pulled the limp man onto the floor. Beel crawled in to help. Together, the four officers dragged the unconscious man into the hallway. Then a firefighter in protective gear emerged through the smoke. A team of firefighters carried the man out of the burning building, and extinguished the fire. SEND US A TIP The rescued resident was transported to a hospital, then transferred to a regional burn center. His name and the cause of the fire have not been released because those details are part of an active investigation. GOT A TIP? Three of the police officers also were treated at a hospital for smoke inhalation and other injuries. They were released that evening. All four who braved the smoke and flames were honored with valor awards on Oct. 14, Capt. Kevin Tooley of the Culpeper Police Department told Fox News Digital. He was a supervisor on the scene. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "They went above and beyond the normal call for a police department," Tooley said of his team. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We normally don't go into burning buildings. I mean, that's not our job. That's typically the fire department's job. But we don't know how to say no, especially when there's a life … that we know we have to save."

articles.title: Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?
articles.summary: Akhlaghi’s experience centres on ballistic missiles, aerospace technology and defence-industrial production.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi has been appointed Iran’s defence minister at a time when the war with the United States is expected to escalate.

The 68-year-old was approved on Sunday by parliament, which has convened online since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28, to assume leadership of the Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics. In total, 237 lawmakers voted in favour of Akhlaghi’s appointment and 15 against.

Former Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed along with a large number of other senior figures, including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, on the opening day of the war.

The position was filled temporarily by Majid Ebn-e Reza, who will now become Akhlaghi’s deputy.

Akhlaghi will be responsible for rebuilding and expanding Iran’s military-industrial infrastructure, which has been heavily targeted by the US and Israel.

The new minister’s defence plans were approved earlier by senior military authorities, President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliament’s Commission on National Security and Foreign Policy.

“The Islamic Republic of Iran will not be the instigator of aggression against any country but will defend the territorial integrity of the country strongly and to the death against any aggression,” Pezeshkian said.

The president said Akhlaghi has more than 42 years of experience in the Defence Ministry and related organisations.

His principal expertise is in ballistic missiles, solid-fuel propulsion, aerospace technology and military-industrial production, according to state media.

Previously, he served as the head of the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, the Aerospace Industries Organization and the Defence Industries Organization. Akhlaghi and these entities are all subject to sanctions by the US. He is also under United Nations sanctions.

He has been associated with developing several missile types and related weapons-development projects over the past decades, according to Tasnim, a newspaper linked with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)

Akhlaghi reportedly played a role in expanding the major Sejjil and Zolfaghar family of Iranian ballistic missiles as well as precision-guided weapons, such as the Almas missiles and Yasin guided bombs.

He is also said to have expertise in space launchers, research rockets and infrastructure associated with the Imam Khomeini Space Center in Semnan. These have all been critical elements in Iran’s wars against Israel and the US.

This month, Iran’s Defence Ministry spokesman, Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik, told reporters that Akhlaghi’s nomination reflected Iran’s need to increase the quantity and quality of strategic weapons, particularly missiles and drones.

“Offensive arms are being actively improved,” the spokesman said.

The US has repeatedly claimed that it has destroyed most of Iran’s military-industrial capacities, but Tehran has maintained it continues to have considerable offensive and defensive capabilities outside the reach of US and Israeli bombs. These weapons have been upgraded based on Iran’s new war experience, it has insisted.

Akhlaghi told members of parliament this month that he had met with senior military commanders, including the commander-in-chief of the IRGC, Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi, to develop a better understanding of their requirements during and after the war.

His priorities as defence minister would be faster military-industrial development, air defences, incorporation of emerging technologies using government and private sector firms, improvements in armed-forces welfare and development of international military cooperation, according to reports.

In his first comments as defence minister on Sunday, Akhlaghi taunted the administration of US President Donald Trump, which this month threatened to use the “mother of all bombs” on Iran’s nuclear and energy infrastructure.

“We have made preparations and continue our work with ease of mind,” he told reporters. “The US president must think of getting his forces out of our region in one piece. If he drops one bomb, he must see how many of his troops he will have to evacuate horizontally.”

articles.title: This year, an Alabama longleaf pine stump revealed a fire scar dating to 1697; a separate Pennsylvania study traced fires back to 1402
articles.summary: A remarkable discovery in Alabama highlights ancient fire scars dating back to 1402, shedding light on Indigenous forest management techniques and the historical significance of fire in shaping landscapes.
articles.body: Evidence of events that occurred centuries before they were written down can be preserved on an ancient tree stump. Researchers may identify when a tree survived a burn and recreate how frequently woods were originally burnt by looking for fire traces inside its growth rings. Another element of that history was unearthed in 2026, when researchers studied remnants of longleaf pine in Alabama’s Flagg Mountain area. Eventually, one old tree was dated to 1612, with its oldest growth and a fire scar in 1697. Fire scars dating to 1402 have been discovered in north-central Pennsylvania, providing one of the longest records of historical fire in eastern North America.Taken together, the results show how tree rings can tell us the function that periodic fires had in forming forests long before modern forest management. They also show indications of a deeper awareness of Indigenous land stewardship, including the practice of purposeful burning to maintain landscapes, encourage valuable flora and aid hunting.What the old stump revealedFieldwork in Alabama focused on old longleaf pine remnants on Flagg Mountain in the southern Appalachian region. Researchers studying the landscape were hunting for relics of trees that had lived long enough to record evidence from before European settlement reshaped much of the region. Longleaf pine historically dominated the southeastern United States. Mature trees have thick bark and other features that allow them to survive multiple low-intensity surface fires. If flames burn around the root of a tree, a small patch of living tissue may be damaged, but the tree may not die. As the tree grows on, the injury is encircled with new wood.A cross section can therefore display the annual growth rings and the scars from previous fires. The rings are dated, and their patterns are compared to other tree-ring data to assign calendar years. This is called cross-dating and is especially helpful when an old stump can't be accurately dated just by looking at it. In Alabama, the reconstructed record shows growth of one tree in the early 17th century and detected a fire scar in 1697. That date is considerably before modern fire suppression policies were established in the United States, yet a scar alone cannot tell who caused the fire or whether it was deliberate.The Pennsylvania record provides a separate, longer chronology. A 2022 study published in Fire Ecology reconstructed red-pine fire history in north-central Pennsylvania from 1402 to 1966. The researchers identified 1,285 fire scars representing 155 distinct fire years across 565 years of recorded fire history.The Significance of Fire in Pine ForestsBefore the era of widespread fire suppression, many woods and woodlands across the southeastern United States were subject to recurrent low-intensity fires. Lightning may ignite them, but Indigenous societies also employed fire to govern landscapes. The relative importance of natural and human-caused fires varied by location and period. Frequent surface fires in longleaf pine ecosystems maintain a relatively open understory. They control numerous fire-sensitive shrubs and trees, minimise accumulated plant detritus, and provide environments for grasses and other native ground cover to thrive. Mature longleaf pines are relatively resistant to these fires, although competing vegetation may be more susceptible.That doesn’t mean every blaze of the past was of the same purpose or intensity. Indigenous tribes used fire for a variety of purposes, including to clear vegetation to facilitate access, to influence the availability of plants and to attract or manage game. Their activities were informed by knowledge of the seasons, the weather, the plants, and the areas they lived in. A separate reconstruction from Louisiana helps illustrate how frequently fire returned to longleaf pine forests. Published in the Journal of Vegetation Science in 2011, the study analyzed 190 fire scars from 19 remnant pines. It found a mean interval of 2.2 years between fires from 1650 to 1905, although intervals ranged from six months to 12 years.The Louisiana data aren’t observations from Alabama, but they do demonstrate how often fires might return to a longleaf pine environment. These data help researchers understand why longleaf forests evolved features that allow older trees to withstand repeated fires and why long-term fire exclusion can modify the structure of these habitats.What the scars can and cannot tellTree rings give a more accurate history of fire than written records alone. A dated scar can tell us that a fire got to a certain tree in a certain year. Researchers can compare scars across numerous trees to determine years in which many trees were impacted, estimate the intervals between reported fires, and study whether burning occurred during the growing or dormant season. A larger collection of records also helps scientists separate local events from broader patterns. The U.S. Geological Survey’s North American tree-ring fire-scar network brings together evidence from more than 37,000 fire-scarred trees across 2,562 sites. These records help scientists examine fire frequency, seasonality and relationships with vegetation, climate and human land use.Even with these records, it is still difficult to know where a given fire started. A fire scar doesn’t indicate if a flame was sparked by lightning, an Indigenous land management method or some other human action. Stronger conclusions will need many lines of data, including the timing and pattern of fires, the ecology of the region and historical and Indigenous knowledge. The 1697 scar provides physical evidence that a fire reached the tree, but it cannot identify who or what started it. Although historical evidence shows that Indigenous communities used fire to manage some landscapes, attributing this particular fire to human activity would require additional evidence.Researchers are also interested in the information Indigenous populations have today. Some groups are reviving cultural burning practices that were lost through colonial relocation and subsequent fire suppression. In Alabama, the connection between traditional stewardship and longleaf pine restoration is especially essential as many of the fire-dependent ecosystems of the region have been diminished via logging, conversion of land and the cessation of regular burning. The Alabama stump and the Pennsylvania red-pine record provide two distinct pieces of evidence about historical fire. The Alabama tree records a fire in 1697, while the Pennsylvania chronology reaches back to 1402. Together with wider fire-scar research and Indigenous knowledge, these records help researchers reconstruct how recurring fires shaped forests over centuries.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Egypt on Sunday announced that it was ready to militarily assist Saudi Arabia for safeguarding its security and stability, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis
articles.body: Egypt on Sunday announced that it was ready to militarily assist Saudi Arabia for safeguarding its security and stability, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis step up their assaults on the world’s largest oil exporter.Sisi has asked for an urgent parliamentary session to authorise the military, one of the largest and most powerful in the region, to help defend Saudi Arabia should the kingdom request its assistance.“Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites,” the Egyptian Presidency said in a statement, according to Reuters.The statement came after a meeting of Egypt’s National Defence Council, which was chaired by President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi. The parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief also attended.In a speech on Saturday, Sisi said Egypt would act in line with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The crown prince had visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen flared up again.In recent days, the Houthis have targeted Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco. The attacks come amid renewed clashes with the Saudi-backed forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, following the collapse of a truce.Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. After the military removal of Islamist President Mohamed Morsi in 2013, Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states supplied Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments.Egypt had earlier joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to back the government against the Houthis, although its combat role was limited.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukraine strikes St Petersburg with over 1,000 drones
articles.summary: Ukraine launched a massive drone attack on Russia overnight Sunday, striking a major oil terminal in St. Petersburg and a data center, knocking out power to thousands of residents and causing fires. Russian state media described the attack as “one of the biggest drone attacks of the year,” according to a translation from Russian. One…
articles.body:
Ukraine launched a massive drone attack on Russia overnight Sunday, striking a major oil terminal in St. Petersburg and a data center, knocking out power to thousands of residents and causing fires.

Russian state media described the attack as “one of the biggest drone attacks of the year,” according to a translation from Russian.

One person was killed and five people were injured, St. Petersburg Gov. Alexander Beglov confirmed in a post on Telegram , adding that buildings and residential homes were also damaged in the aerial attack.

“Emergency services continue to work on extinguishing fires at the St. Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky District,” he wrote.

In the surrounding Leningrad region, Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said two electrical substations were struck, leaving roughly 20,000 residents without power Sunday morning.

The strikes come as Russia and Ukraine resume attacks on one another’s energy infrastructure, despite repeated warnings from President Trump to stop, blaming the strikes for rising fuel prices.

The strikes occurred days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had ordered the military to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries following a brief pause under an energy ceasefire announced by Trump.

Trump said last weekend that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop targeting each other’s energy infrastructure following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

But Zelensky accused Moscow of continuing to strike Ukrainian power facilities, violating the announced agreement.

On Sunday, the Ukrainian leader said Russia had carried out at least 76 attacks on Ukrainian energy, oil and gas facilities over the past week, leaving tens of thousands of households without electricity.

Zelensky said Russian forces had launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles at Ukraine over the past week.

“The Russians are trying to cause a blackout,” he wrote on the social platform X . “And America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements.”
