articles.title: US judge dismisses Trump admin bid to overturn New York City sanctuary policies
articles.summary: A federal judge has dismissed the Trump administration's bid to invalidate New York City's sanctuary policies, reinforcing local authorities' ability to refuse federal immigration enforcement. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani praised the ruling as a victory for community unity.
articles.body: A federal judge has dismissed the Trump administration’s attempt to overturn New York City’s sanctuary policies, ruling that local authorities cannot be compelled to use their staff and resources to enforce federal civil immigration laws.The ruling, issued on Thursday by US District Judge Ramón E Reyes Jr, was welcomed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who said the city would not allow immigration enforcement to create divisions among its residents.“The federal government came to court seeking to force New York City to turn its public servants into deportation agents and divert our resources toward carrying out ICE’s cruel agenda,” Mamdani said in a statement.He added that the city would continue to protect its residents, saying: “Our city belongs to all of us, and we will not abandon our neighbors to satisfy an inhumane, xenophobic agenda.”In his ruling, Reyes said federal law did not require states to take part in immigration enforcement or comply with federal requests to do so. The judge rejected the administration’s argument that New York City’s policies unlawfully interfered with its immigration operations.“There is nothing within federal law that obligates states to participate in federal immigration enforcement or compels states to comply,” Reyes wrote.The lawsuit was part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to challenge policies that limit cooperation between local authorities and federal immigration agencies. Similar cases brought against Los Angeles, Chicago and Minnesota have also been dismissed by federal courts in recent years.New York City’s sanctuary rules restrict how local agencies cooperate with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), including limits on holding people in custody solely on the basis of ICE detainer requests and sharing certain information with federal authorities.The Justice Department had argued in its original complaint that the city’s policies allowed people accused or convicted of crimes to be released when they could otherwise have been held for immigration removal. The department had not immediately responded to a request for comment following Thursday’s ruling.The ruling comes amid renewed attention on the relationship between New York City police and federal immigration authorities. Earlier this month, an ICE agent shot 28-year-old Oscar Belgal while his child was in the back of his car, after which the agency detained him.The New York Police Department arrived at the scene and later faced criticism over its handling of protests, including an incident involving Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier. She said the police response violated “the spirit, if not the letter” of the city’s sanctuary laws.Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said on Thursday that the NYPD had not been involved in the federal immigration operation before the shooting. She said officers attended the scene to preserve evidence.Although the administration lost its challenge to New York City’s policies, it has continued to expand a separate programme that allows local police departments to take on federal immigration enforcement duties.Under agreements known as 287(g), local officers can be authorised to enforce federal immigration law. New York City does not have such an agreement, but the American Civil Liberties Union has documented the programme’s expansion across the country during the second Trump administration.You use AI every day. articles.title: Macron to address nation after riots and looting lead to 1,800 arrests across France
articles.summary: PARIS — Police arrested at least 1,800 people across France after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during nationwide demonstrations that drew hundreds of thousands protesting rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
articles.body: PARIS — Police arrested at least 1,800 people across France after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during nationwide demonstrations that drew hundreds of thousands protesting rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. President Emmanuel Macron was due to hold an emergency meeting with senior government officials on Sunday before addressing the nation at 8 p.m., his office said. Masked groups set fires and attacked public buildings, including city halls, in several cities on Saturday, authorities said. In the central city of Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building. Hundreds of protesters gathered again Sunday at the Place de la République in Paris amid a heavy police presence. Officers used tear gas as tensions flared sporadically. “The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, citing the looting of hundreds of businesses in cities including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux. About 550,000 people took part in protests across France, according to authorities, while organizers put the figure at about 800,000. Demonstrators answered calls from a labor union, student organizations and activists hoping to revive the “yellow vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 to protest social injustice. Mass protests in France are often marred by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police. The arrest tally reported Sunday approached the nearly 2,000 recorded nationwide during a single day of yellow vest protests in December 2018. One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said in a statement, without providing details. The Paris prosecutor’s office said it was investigating. Parisians deplore shattered shops and a damaged square Dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass littered the area around Paris’ Place de la République on Sunday. Looting and damage were also reported in other tourist and shopping districts. Paris police said 855 people were arrested in the capital region. The city’s prosecutor’s office said 557 remained in police custody. “I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed,” said government employee Marie Peyreigne, 57, wondering what had led to the mayhem. Parisians inspecting the damage photographed the partially dismantled base of the square’s central monument, a statue of Marianne, a symbol of France. Jean Foissy, 74, said he had wanted to join the protest but encountered “a wall of riot police and fires everywhere” and returned home. “I was very scared,” he said. “I’ve been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me.” Margaux Eude, 26, said she supported the protest movement but “didn’t think it would escalate like this.” “It’s the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimizes the movement,” she said. Political leaders trade blame ahead of presidential election Political leaders across the spectrum sought to parlay the fallout of Saturday’s riots into political capital, looking ahead to next spring’s presidential election. Far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen lashed out at far-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march. “Looting, ransacking, destroying and attacking law enforcement: Rioters have again spoiled the Oct. 17 demonstrations,” Le Pen wrote on X. Her running mate, Jordan Bardella, said on X that “if the silent majority of French decide it, we will reestablish order for the long term.” Mélenchon, for his part, accused Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of “playing with fire,” alleging that “by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers’ unions.” Mélenchon insisted that “my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction.” U.S. President Donald Trump posted “France is burning!” on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to “the immigration of people from an entirely different world.” “Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” he wrote. French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting and have repeatedly attributed some of the violence to “radical far-left groups” and other people who joined to loot. Hundreds of businesses looted across the country “The scale of the damage is considerable and unprecedented,” Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire wrote in an open letter. “Paris is a city of freedoms, debate and demonstrations. It must remain so. But it must also be a city where everyone can work and run a business safely.” Police said groups of hundreds of people formed unauthorized marches across central Paris on Saturday. “By late afternoon, a new phase began with the arrival of large numbers of people whose sole aim was to steal and loot, taking advantage of the unrest,” police said. The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, the three largest cities, requested a meeting with the prime minister in the coming days “given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation.” In the southern port city of Marseille, some protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall and a group of people wearing hoods and masks damaged a police station. In Lyon, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.

Student unions originally initiated the movement to protest underfunding, deteriorating infrastructure, and acute teacher shortages across French high schools and universities. By joining the protests, the Gilets Jaunes introduce their established platform against austerity cuts, rising living costs, and surging fuel prices into the youth-led action. articles.title: Search for Amelia Earhart's plane resumes after stormy weather
articles.summary: An expedition to a remote Pacific island hoping to uncover the American aviator's wreckage was on hold for three days.
articles.body:
A search for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote island in the Pacific Ocean has resumed after severe weather caused researchers to stop for several days.

A team has travelled to Nikumaroro Island, part of Kiribati, hoping to solve the mystery of the famed aviator's disappearance by investigating the so-called Taraia Object, spotted in the atoll's lagoon in aerial imagery.

The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation about her fate.

Rough seas and strong winds forced the team to remain on their research vessel for three days, until the weather cleared on Sunday.

"We are finally getting off the ship and able to land on Nikumaroro," Sirisha Bandla, a technology specialist who is part of the expedition, said in a video update from the deck of the Marin Mainiku.

The researchers arrived at the uninhabited atoll last week and began an underwater survey of the area of interest.

But the weather - powered by strong El Niño conditions in the Pacific - has so far prevented them from beginning a second of three phases, in which underwater objects will be probed to determine their depth and sediment will be dredged.

"We're working to get everything done today if we can," Bandla said. "The crew's really excited."

Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.

From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.

But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.

One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.

Images of the so-called Taraia Object - which Purdue University says is visible in photography dating back to 1938 - show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters, though other explorers remain sceptical .

Interest in the expedition prompted New Zealand's Air Force Museum to publish previously unseen reconnaissance images of Nikumaroro on Friday.

While the Taraia Object is not obviously visible in any of the black-and-white slides, taken in 1938 from a seaplane, they do show the beached wreck of the SS Norwich City, a British merchant vessel that ran aground on the island during a storm in 1929, killing 11.

Purdue, which with the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) is spearheading the expedition, said the incident demonstrated the risks surrounding the island.

To get into the atoll's lagoon, a boat has to navigate through a narrow gap created in the reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.

But the university said wind gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph) present around the island until Sunday meant the transport boat could be knocked into the reef by crashing waves.

However, it said the Norwich City wreck may lend credence to the researchers' theory.

Purdue said a 15-year-old in Florida reported hearing Earhart's voice repeating "New York City" over her father's shortwave radio shortly after the aviator vanished. Proponents of the castaway theory argue this may have been a misunderstanding of Earhart giving her location as near the Norwich City.

As a result of the three-day hold, the research team has extended the expedition time to complete its fieldwork and has yet to indicate whether they had found any promising evidence of Earhart's plane.

ALI director Rick Pettigrew said the team was aware of the global interest in the expedition and would share its results "as soon as we are able". Purdue suggested before the poor weather hit that it could identify the Taraia Object in a matter of days.

While researchers have previously found evidence of a human presence on the island around the time of Earhart's disappearance, some skeptics believe the Taraia Object was just a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the lagoon.

Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.

In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.

Similarly, an expedition in 2019 to investigate a photograph of what might have been landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.

articles.title: Arizona man threatened with arrest for preaching at holiday festival files lawsuit
articles.summary: David Hoffman alleges Tucson police told him discussing Jesus at the Winterhaven Festival of Lights would be considered "sermonizing" under a new policy.
articles.body: An Arizona street evangelist is suing the city of Tucson and challenging an event policy barring religious speech after police officers threatened to arrest him for discussing Jesus at an annual holiday festival. David Hoffman has been evangelizing at public events for over a decade and views large public gatherings as crucial to his Christian ministry. "What we do is we share the gospel with people that are most likely never going to go into a church, and we go to events and places where there's not already a Christian witness, and we have conversations," he told Fox News Digital. For nearly ten years, Hoffman regularly attended Tuscon's Winterhaven Festival of Lights, a free holiday event where thousands of visitors walk through a residential neighborhood to view light displays. But during the December 2025 festival, Hoffman said city police officers barred him from sharing his faith and threatened him with criminal trespassing charges under new event rules. GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS "Upon entering the event, we were told that we can't have any kind of religious expression," Hoffman told Fox News Digital. "They said that you can be there to participate in looking at the lights. But the moment, you know, we tried to talk to somebody or give out a gospel tract, that would lead to a violation of what they were enforcing." According to a federal lawsuit filed on Hoffman’s behalf by First Liberty Institute, the city of Tucson adopted an event solicitation policy last year prohibiting "religious, political, or issue-based leafleting" with signs posted at entrances relaying these prohibitions and warning that violators could face removal and trespassing charges enforced by Tucson police. When Hoffman attempted to speak with attendees, officers approached Hoffman and said he could not be inside "doing the preaching." When Hoffman asked if his volume was an issue, an officer explained that "it's the sending of your message, which is one of the prohibited rules," according to the complaint. The officer went on to tell Hoffman that asking someone if they would like to discuss Jesus amounted to "sermonizing," adding that "once you start sermonizing, that becomes a problem," according to the complaint. SUPREME COURT UNANIMOUSLY SLAPS DOWN BLUE STATE TARGETING PRO-LIFE GROUP "At one point, Hoffman is stopped by a couple of police," First Liberty legal counsel Garrett Bell told Fox News Digital. "And he says, 'Well, what if someone comes up to me and asks me, how can I be saved? Can I respond to them?' And the officers told him, 'No, if you want to have that conversation with them, you're going to have to step outside the perimeter of the event.'" According to the complaint, officers and an event organizer told Hoffman the speech restrictions were city policy established in response to past complaints. After repeated warnings, four uniformed Tucson police officers escorted Hoffman out of the festival under threat of arrest. Officers told him he could preach in a designated "free expression zone" outside the festival perimeter, according to the complaint. "When I saw it, it kind of looked like a cage because they had these barricades set up, and they said, 'You can be in that corner over there,'" Hoffman said. "And it felt kind of, just really, it felt funny because it's like, you know, putting the Christians over kind of in this specific area." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE First Liberty alleges the barricaded zone was set up alongside a busy street which made engaging in conversations with people passing by impractical. The legal group says commercial food vendors, live performers, and 15-passenger "pedal pub" party bikes playing amplified music were permitted throughout the festival area. In December 2025, First Liberty sent a demand letter to Tucson on Hoffman's behalf, warning the city that its policy was unconstitutional, but the group said it received no response. First Liberty filed a complaint against the city this week, alleging the policy violates Hoffman's First Amendment rights to free speech and the free exercise of religion, the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause and the Arizona Constitution. The complaint asks for preliminary and permanent injunctive relief to allow Hoffman to share the gospel at this year's event, and a declaratory judgment that the policy is unconstitutional. TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS "This event is happening on city streets and city sidewalks, and in constitutional law, those areas, along with, say, a public park, offer the most constitutional protection of any location you can be at," Bell said. He also argued that the city's policy singles out religious viewpoints. "You can talk about the weather. You can talk about the Arizona Cardinals or the U of A Wildcats, but you can't talk about religion," he added. "Censoring a Christian message during a public Christmas event is malicious, unconstitutional, and absurd," Nate Kellum, senior counsel at First Liberty, said in a statement. "A public street festival is just that – a public space where citizens can visit, walk around, and converse with each other about different ideas. The government cannot ban only religious messages." The complaint names the city of Tucson and Tucson PD officers Matt Alexander and William Leonard, in their individual capacities, as defendants. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The city of Tucson said it does not comment on pending litigation.The Tucson PD did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Kyiv apologises again as Russia diverts Ukrainian drones into Baltic states; what is GPS spoofing
articles.summary: Ukraine apologised to Lithuania on Sunday after its drones may have strayed into Lithuanian airspace during an operation against Russian military targets.
articles.body: Ukraine apologised to Lithuania on Sunday after its drones may have strayed into Lithuanian airspace during an operation against Russian military targets. Ukraine's foreign ministry said the incident may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare. The apology comes amid repeated drone incursions into Baltic airspace and Lithuania's warning that Russia can falsify GPS signals across a radius of up to 450 km from its Kaliningrad exclave."We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia," spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi wrote on X."We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused. We are committed to sharing all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident."An earlier version of Tykhyi's post also mentioned Latvia.Russia expands GPS spoofing network near Baltic statesRussia has increased the number of GPS spoofing antennae in its Kaliningrad exclave from three in early 2025 to 36 now, Darius Kuliesius, deputy head of Lithuania's communications regulator, told Reuters on Tuesday.Kaliningrad is a heavily militarised Russian territory between NATO members Lithuania and Poland on the Baltic coast. Kuliesius said Russia's GPS spoofing capability could reach up to 450 km from the exclave."The occasional interference began with the 2023 NATO summit in Vilnius. Now they have built up the infrastructure and the interference has become systemic, permanent, unending Russian provocation against European security," Kuliesius said.A map from Lithuania's regulator indicated that the interference could reach across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, most of Poland, and parts of Finland, Sweden and Belarus, as well as the Baltic Sea.The regulator estimated the range by analysing disturbances in aviation surveillance ADS-B transmissions, Kuliesius said.Russia has frequently denied accusations of electronic interference. The Russian embassy in Vilnius did not immediately respond to a request for comment.What is GPS spoofing?GPS spoofing involves broadcasting false GPS signals to confuse navigation systems. Kuliesius said Russia's expanded antenna network could falsify signals across a radius of up to 450 km from Kaliningrad.The interference has also affected mobile phone networks near Kaliningrad, degrading their quality on some frequencies, Kuliesius said. He added that spoofing and jamming intensify during Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia."Online bus schedules in Klaipeda stop working during the spikes, because they rely on tracking buses by GPS", he said, referring to a town 50 km from the Kaliningrad border.Most modern passenger aircraft and major airports have a variety of navigation tools available if GPS encounters problems.NATO jet shoots down suspected Ukrainian drone over EstoniaOn May 19, a Romanian NATO fighter jet shot down a suspected Ukrainian drone over Estonia after it entered the country's airspace from Russia, the Estonian military said.The drone entered southeastern Estonia around noon local time and was shot down at 12.14 pm with a single missile."The incident occurred under the conditions of heavy electronic warfare, including GPS spoofing and jamming, by Russia," the Estonian military said.NATO confirmed that a Romanian jet had shot down a drone over Estonian airspace and said an investigation was under way. It also said the alliance was ready and able to respond to potential air threats.Latvia issued an air threat alert on the same day after a drone entered its airspace. Residents near the Russian border were told to stay indoors, while NATO Baltic Air Policing jets were summoned to the area.The alert led to train suspensions, the stoppage of national examinations for ninth-grade students and the closure of grocery shops, according to local media reports. It was not immediately clear whether the drone that entered Latvia was the same one reported in Estonia or a separate aircraft.Both Baltic countries blamed the incursions on Moscow and said Ukraine had the right to strike Russian military targets to weaken Russia's ability to wage war. They stressed that they had not allowed Ukraine to launch attacks on Russia from their territories.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the previous week that Ukraine would send experts to Latvia to help protect its skies.Previous GPS interference affected European leaders' flightsLast year, a Spanish military jet carrying Defence Minister Margarita Robles experienced GPS disruption near Kaliningrad. A plane carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was also jammed while travelling to Bulgaria.Estonia and Finland have also blamed Russia for jamming GPS navigation devices in the region's airspace.On May 15, Finnish authorities warned of suspected drone activity in the country's capital region. Helsinki airport suspended traffic for three hours, while the Finnish defence forces scrambled fighter jets and other emergency services. No drones were eventually found.Since March, several Ukrainian military drones have strayed into the airspace of NATO members Finland, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, all of which border Russia. Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russia, including around the Baltic region.The Latvian government resigned the week before the May 19 incidents over its handling of the drone incursions.

articles.title: Tirana sees sixth day of violent protests as Albania’s PM refuses to resign
articles.summary: Police crack down on hundreds of protesters in Albania’s capital, using rubber bullets, water cannons and tear gas.
articles.body:
Violent protests have rocked Albania’s capital Tirana for the sixth consecutive day as Prime Minister Edi Rama, who is serving his fourth term, ruled out resigning.

Hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday in front of the Ministry of Education, chanting “Rama, resign” in a tense standoff with the police, who later used rubber bullets, water cannons and tear gas to hold back the crowds.

Shops and institutions in the centre of the city have secured their doors and windows with metal shutters, while city workers removed paving stones to prevent their use by protesters.

Lindita Karadaku, a journalist for Albanian news outlet TV Klan, told Al Jazeera on Sunday that it was difficult to see how the unrest could unfold or how long it could last.

“Prime Minister Rama is determined and has made it very clear that he will not resign, but also the young people who are protesting are determined and make it clear that they will not give up so easily,” she said. “At this moment, no one is clear what tomorrow will bring.”

Rama said during a live social media stream on Sunday that “the government is not being challenged” but implied that ongoing unrest in the country might affect Albania’s path towards European Union membership.

“Albanians need to think very clearly,” Rama said. “⁠Do they want this, or do they want the EU?”

Albania is hoping to achieve membership status by 2030.

Protesters are demanding better education, more jobs, a stop to alleged ongoing corruption, and Rama’s resignation.

According to local media reports, demonstrators in Tirana were primarily attacking government institutions and the police, including the Ministry of Education building and the area around Rama’s office.

The prime minister, who has been in office since 2013, blamed the involvement of a “foreign hand” for the surge in protests and said his government is doing its best to address corruption.

At the same time, he said that he was ready to listen to the justified demands of students and discuss the costs of education. But he insisted that those responsible for the destruction of property must be held accountable.

According to a Ministry of Health report issued on Sunday morning, 65 people were injured, of which 37 were police officers, while 12 were hospitalised. Since Tuesday, 272 people have been injured in the clashes, including 169 police officers, the ministry said.

Discontent in Albania has been growing for months. The first protests in the country this year were called the “Flamingo Revolution” and began in May. Demonstrators rebelled against the controversial project of a luxury tourist complex in the south of Albania, affiliated with Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.

articles.title: Trump endorses Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of pivotal Israeli election
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday for the upcoming Israeli parliamentary election.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday for the upcoming Israeli parliamentary election. “Bibi ⁠Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” ⁠Trump wrote in ​a post ⁠on Truth Social. “This is the kind of Partner that ⁠the United States of America is demanding ​of ⁠Israel, a Country ‌for which it has done so much. Please let this Letter serve to ‌represent my Complete and Total ‌Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.” Israel ⁠will hold a national election on October 27, its first vote since the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023 that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as ‌Israel went to war in Gaza, ​Lebanon and Iran. The election will ‌determine whether Netanyahu ⁠remains in power after one of ⁠the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, or is ‌defeated by ​centrist rivals promising ‌to usher in a ​new era. It is not typical for U.S. presidents to make explicit endorsements in foreign elections, but Trump has done so on a number of occasions.

articles.title: CJP's Dipke accuses state of delaying proceedings to prevent release of Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke on Sunday accused the state of intentionally prolonging Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka's arrest in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke on Sunday accused the state of intentionally prolonging Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka's arrest in order to delay court proceedings and delay their release."The state is deliberately prolonging Ashu and Saurav’s illegal arrest by using every dirty trick in the book to delay court proceedings and prevent their release," Dipke said in an X post."They have no legal grounds to keep them behind bars, so they are resorting to delaying tactics to keep them there," he added.On October 14, Das and Ranka were sent to five days of judicial custody after they entered Jantar Mantar, a site denotified for designated protest, by scaling its locked gates. The CJP leaders said they had unfurled the national flag and raised slogans.CJP's legal head Ratna Singh, who was present in the court for hearing on the matter accused the Special Executive Magistrate of "arbitrary remarks" and deliberately delaying the hearing, PTI reported."We have been here since morning. We were told that the entire hearing would take place at 12.00 pm. Today, everything was complete, the verification was done, and all requirements were met. We have been waiting here since noon. The SEM (Special Executive Magistrate) was at the police station by 1:30 pm, but he did not enter the courtroom until 5.00 pm," Singh said, as per PTI."When he finally arrived, he refused to hear our case on its merits regarding whether Saurav and Ashutosh should be released from judicial custody. Instead, he made arbitrary remarks," she added.Singh alleged that within about five minutes of the proceedings, the SEM told the court that he had received a threatening message. From that point onwards, the entire discussion was focused solely on the message."It is clear that this entire episode was orchestrated," Singh alleged, "They had decided beforehand to come into the courtroom and focus exclusively on this alleged threatening message, completely bypassing whether the formalities required for Saurav and Ashutosh's release were fulfilled."There was no response from police on the allegations yet. PTI reportedOn Saturday, the CJP said in a post on X that it had consulted senior advocate Kapil Sibal and warned of legal action if Das and Ranka were not released by Sunday.“If Ashu and Saurav are not released by tomorrow, we will pursue legal action against all those who deliberately ensured that they continue to be in illegal custody, especially when they have not committed nor charged with any offence,” the outfit said.“The deliberate use of delaying tactics to keep them behind bars cannot go unchallenged. Those responsible will be held accountable,” it added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Mother and daughter found murdered while family mourned another loss. 37 years later, questions remain
articles.summary: Mother and daughter, Ann Furst and Helen Larkin were found bludgeoned to death at Ann’s home in Aberdeen, Maryland, in 1989. No suspects have been named. The Harford County Sheriff’s Office is investigating.
articles.body: There are days that stick with a person. Days of celebration, days of achievement, and days of mourning. For cousins Maribeth Ryan and Matthew Kineke, October 1989 was a time of mourning. Their grandfather, Rudolf Furst, had died. But before they could lay him to rest, tragedy would strike their family again, leaving them with decades of unanswered questions. Rudolf and his wife, Ann Furst, were both immigrants. Rudolph came to the United States from Germany, Ann from what was then Czechoslovakia. Ann and her first husband arrived with their young daughter, Wilma, Matthew’s mother. Two years later, Ann gave birth to Maribeth’s mother, Helen. Following her divorce, Ann met Rudolf in New York City, where they both had thriving careers. After they married, the couple moved to Maryland to be closer to Wilma. “Some of my earliest memories are of going by Grandma and Grandpa’s, or as my father called them, ‘G and G,’” Matthew told Dateline. He grew up on the outskirts of Aberdeen, not far from his grandparents. Maribeth’s mother, Helen Larkin, was an artist. She worked with watercolors, and even brought Maribeth to the studio. “Quite often when I was younger, I would be, like, the model. And she would take me to classes, and they would paint me,” Maribeth said. Like her mother, Helen met her future husband in New York City. Both were art students, and he studied oil pastels. Maribeth says both of her parents were passionate artists and the family has held onto many of their paintings. Though Maribeth says her extended family wasn’t particularly close, she has great memories of her grandparents, especially visits to her grandmother’s house in Aberdeen. “She had rose gardens, and it was always such a lovely place to visit.” Matthew remembers the roses, too. “She was zen in the art of rosebushes,” he said. “Her roses were just these enormous, healthy, vigorous plants.” In October 1989, Rudolf Furst died of cancer. On October 17, following his wake in Aberdeen, family members gathered at Matthew’s parents’ home. “It was my mother and father, myself, my mother’s sister Helen, and their mother, Ann Furst,” Matthew said. His aunt Helen had driven down that day from Connecticut and was going to be staying with his grandmother, Ann. “I actually said good night to them, um, you know, let them talk a little bit,” Matthew said. “I heard them get ready to leave and came to the top of the stairs.” He said goodbye to his aunt and grandmother, not knowing that would be the last time he would see them alive. The next morning, Helen’s daughter, Maribeth, drove to Aberdeen with her father and brothers for Rudolf’s funeral. “I was at University of Delaware. My two brothers and my father were in Connecticut, so they drove down, picked me up at Delaware, and then we drove down to Maryland,” Maribeth said. They planned to stop at Ann’s house to pick up her mother and grandmother and head to the funeral. “When we got there, my mom’s car was in the driveway. We just assumed everything was normal. And so we knocked, ‘knock, knock,’ on the door. It was locked,” Maribeth said. No one came to the door. One of her brothers went around the back of the house to see if he could get in through the sliding glass door. What he found was horrifying. The sliding door was shattered. Maribeth’s brother climbed through the broken glass door and let everyone inside. Glass covered the living room floor, and the TV was on. Down the hall, Helen and Ann were dead in the primary bedroom. “My father tried to get me out very quickly, and my older brother, Jim, called 911,” Maribeth said. It was just after 10 a.m. when the Harford County Sheriff’s Office arrived at the scene. Detective Patrick Ross told Dateline a brick was discovered underneath the dining room table. “The brick was actually taken from a neighbor’s flower bed and used to shatter the glass,” he said. Around that time, Matthew’s family learned what had happened. Matthew was in the kitchen getting ready to leave for the funeral when the phone rang. It was Maribeth’s father. “My uncle said, ‘Matt, this is your Uncle Dick. Let me speak to your father right away.’” Matthew remembers handing the phone to his dad. “He said, ‘Yeah, Dick, what’s up?’ And then, like two seconds later, I saw my father slump against the -- against the door jamb there in the kitchen. Like, I thought he might have had a heart attack or something,” Matthew remembered. “And at that moment, my mother came into the kitchen, looked at my father, and immediately concluded, and effectively knew, that -- that her mother was gone.” Detective Ross confirmed that Ann Furst and her daughter Helen were found in Ann’s bedroom. Both women were in their nightgowns. Ann was on the floor next to her bed. “She had multiple, um, head wounds like she got struck in the head,” he said. “Helen was found in the corner sitting in a chair. And she, again, had multiple head wounds.” Ross says investigators at the time believed the women were killed with a cylindrical weapon, possibly a crowbar. However, the weapon was never found. “There’s really nothing that we could ever determine was left by the suspect,” Ross said. The Harford County Sheriff’s Office gathered what evidence they could. Ross says investigators canvassed the neighborhood and began to piece together a timeline. Neighbors believed Helen and Ann arrived at Ann’s house around 11 p.m. on October 17. “At around 11:30, some neighbors reported hearing what sounded like glass breaking,” Ross said. “Two neighbors talked about hearing what they thought was a woman screaming. So actually around 11:25 to 11:30, I think, is pretty on point to when the murder actually occurred.” The detective added that no 911 calls were received that night from Ann’s neighborhood. Investigators found no evidence of a robbery. Wallets, purses, and Helen’s suitcase were all accounted for. “Nothing appeared as if it was, like, gone through or rummaged through,” Ross said. “Nobody could ever explain what any kind of motive could be.” Maribeth and Matthew both remember being questioned by investigators in the days following the murders. They were asked if anyone came to mind as a suspect, but couldn’t think of anyone. Detective Ross says to this day, no suspects have been named in the case. When Ross took over the case in 2024, he tried to give it new life. “You figure almost every cold case now that’s solved from, like, a significant time period is usually solved by some type of DNA,” he said. “And a large part of what I’ve done over the past two years is review evidence and then send things off. And as of this moment, nothing has [been] determined to have any kind of DNA.” “They’ve reviewed the glass. They’ve reviewed the curtain that was on there. There was, like, a stain on the curtain. It was determined to be, uh, like, dirt, probably from the brick,” Ross said. “But there was never any kind of determination of any kind of blood being on those objects.” He says he’s re-interviewed neighbors, including the couple who owned the house next door where the brick was taken from. “They were never considered suspects. They were talked to like everybody else in the neighborhood, and it just so happened that their brick from their garden appeared to be, uh, taken from there and used to break the slider.” Investigators have also explored whether a serial killer could have been involved. “They actually looked into Tommy Lynn Sells,” Ross said. “He has been tied to a lot of murders. Unfortunately, he’s a serial killer, but he’s also what they call, like, a serial confessor.” Ross says investigators obtained hair from Sells to compare to the crime scene. “Nothing ever pointed to him, and I don’t know if he’s ever really been known to go -- be in Maryland.” Another person investigators looked at was local serial killer Vernon Lee Clark, who was convicted of murdering multiple elderly women in the greater Baltimore area in the 1980s. “I actually kinda looked into him a little bit, but again, there’s really nothing that ties him to Harford County,” Det. Ross said. “Even if you were to come up here, why would you go to that neighborhood, that house, that night?” Ross says Ann Furst’s neighborhood was quiet, quaint, and off the beaten path. Nearly four decades later, investigators have no named suspects, no usable DNA evidence and no clear motive in the killings. “At the time, did I think I’d be -- I’d be left wondering fundamentally who the heck did this for 37 years? No,” Matthew said. “How does somebody break into a house where two older women, elderly women, are getting ready to, like, go to bed, brutally murder them, and then just, like, fade away?” Det. Ross wondered. It’s a question he’ll keep asking himself until the case is solved. “I just want it to end,” Maribeth said. She is hopeful Detective Ross will be the person to solve the case. “I have been through, oh my gosh, maybe a dozen detectives, and he has been the best,” she said. Ross says Maribeth has been instrumental in keeping the case alive. “I just keep pursuing little by little,” Maribeth told Dateline. “We’ll see what happens.” For cousins Matthew and Maribeth, the days of October 1989 have stayed with them for nearly 40 years now. “There are events that fundamentally alter your life,” Matthew said. “My father referred to it as the events of October,” he added. “It’s changed who I have become,” Maribeth said.
